concepts.name: Founding and Early Origins of CPI (1920–1925)
key_dimensions: Tashkent founding (October 1920) by M.N. Roy vs. formal Indian founding at Kanpur (1925) — UPSC trap on 'first' vs. 'official' founding
Role of M.N. Roy, S.A. Dange, Shaukat Usmani, Muzaffar Ahmad as founding figures
Comintern (Communist International) connection and Soviet influence on early CPI ideology
Distinction between CPI's overseas founding context and its domestic organizational emergence

concepts.name: M.N. Roy: Ideological Contributions and Break with Comintern
key_dimensions: Roy's 'Supplementary Theses' at Second Comintern Congress (1920) vs. Lenin's 'Colonial Theses' — nature of disagreement on bourgeois nationalism
Roy's concept of 'New Humanism' and later break from Marxist orthodoxy
Roy's founding of the Radical Democratic Party (1940) as a post-Communist trajectory
UPSC trap: Roy left CPI before it became prominent domestically; his contribution is ideological, not organizational

concepts.name: Peshawar Conspiracy Case and Meerut Conspiracy Case
key_dimensions: Peshawar Conspiracy Case (1922–23): early British suppression of Communist activity on the frontier
Meerut Conspiracy Case (1929–33): arrest of 33 labor and Communist leaders including S.A. Dange, Shaukat Usmani, Philip Spratt
British strategy of using sedition laws to conflate trade unionism with Communist subversion
Paradoxical effect: Meerut trial gave CPI pan-Indian publicity and martyrdom narrative — compare with INC response to the trial

concepts.name: CPI and the Indian National Congress: Collaboration, Tension, and Entry Strategy
key_dimensions: CPI's 'entryism' strategy — joining Congress to work from within during 1930s
Congress Socialist Party (CSP) as an intermediate platform through which Communists operated
Tension over CPI's ultimate loyalty to Comintern directives vs. national movement priorities
INC's eventual expulsion of Communist members from CSP (1940) due to ideological conflicts

concepts.name: CPI's Stance During World War II: 'People's War' Thesis
key_dimensions: Initial anti-war stance (1939–41) aligning with Nazi-Soviet Pact period
Dramatic reversal after Germany invaded USSR (June 1941): CPI declared WWII a 'People's War' and supported British war effort
British legalized CPI in 1942 in exchange for this support — unique position among Indian political parties
CPI's opposition to Quit India Movement (1942) as the single most controversial decision in its history — 'national betrayal' charge by nationalists

concepts.name: CPI and the Quit India Movement (1942): A Critical Divergence
key_dimensions: CPI actively opposed Quit India Movement, calling it adventurist and a distraction from anti-fascist struggle
This placed CPI on the same side as British colonial administration — long-term damage to CPI's nationalist credentials
UPSC trap: CPI was the only major political party to oppose Quit India from a leftist ideological position (Muslim League opposed it for different reasons)
Impact on post-independence perception: CPI's patriotism questioned by mainstream nationalists, affecting electoral prospects

concepts.name: CPI's Position on Pakistan and the Two-Nation Theory
key_dimensions: CPI's 1942 resolution supporting Muslim League's demand for Pakistan based on 'right of self-determination of nationalities'
Ideological basis: Stalin's theory of nationalities applied to Indian subcontinent
UPSC trap: CPI supported Pakistan demand not out of communalism but Stalinist nationality theory — a subtle but examinable distinction
Contrast with INC's rejection of two-nation theory; long-term impact on CPI's image in Hindu nationalist discourse

concepts.name: Telangana Armed Struggle (1946–1951)
key_dimensions: Peasant uprising in Hyderabad's Nizam-ruled Telangana region led by CPI against feudal landlords (Deshmukhs, Doras)
Andhra Mahasabha as the organizational vehicle through which CPI mobilized agrarian discontent
Red Army (guerrilla force) established by CPI — unique instance of armed Communist insurrection in post-independence India
CPI's decision to call off the struggle in 1951 — internal debate between 'Chinese path' (armed revolution) vs. parliamentary path

concepts.name: CPI in the 1952 General Elections: First Electoral Test
key_dimensions: CPI emerged as the single largest opposition party in the first Lok Sabha (1952) with 16 seats
UPSC trap: CPI was the principal opposition, not the Socialist Party, in the first Lok Sabha
CPI's strong performance in Andhra, Bengal, and Kerala — regional concentration of Communist support
Significance: demonstrated viability of parliamentary path, reinforcing the 'revisionist' faction within CPI

concepts.name: Kerala 1957: First Elected Communist Government in the World
key_dimensions: EMS Namboodiripad led CPI to victory in 1957 Kerala elections — first democratically elected Communist government globally
Land reforms, education policy (Vimochana Samaram controversy), and administrative changes attempted
Dismissal of EMS government in 1959 under Article 356 by Nehru government — role of Congress and Church-led agitation
UPSC trap: debate on whether this dismissal was constitutionally justified or politically motivated — landmark in President's Rule jurisprudence

concepts.name: CPI Split of 1964: Formation of CPI(M)
key_dimensions: Root causes: Sino-Soviet split, CPI's pro-Soviet vs. pro-China factions, debate on 'revisionism' vs. revolutionary Marxism
CPI's support for Nehru government (including during 1962 Sino-Indian War) seen as class collaboration by radical faction
The 'left faction' broke away to form Communist Party of India (Marxist) — CPI(M) — in 1964 at Calcutta
UPSC trap: CPI(M) is NOT the same as CPI; they are separate parties with different electoral bases, ideological lines, and coalition histories

concepts.name: Sino-Soviet Split and Its Impact on Indian Communism
key_dimensions: Khrushchev's 'de-Stalinization' and 'peaceful coexistence' thesis vs. Mao's revolutionary line — global ideological fracture
CPI aligned with Soviet 'peaceful parliamentary path'; radical faction aligned with Chinese 'people's war' thesis
CPI's support for India during 1962 war with China further alienated pro-China Communists
Three-way fragmentation: CPI (pro-Soviet), CPI(M) (independent Marxist), CPI(ML) (Naxalite, pro-Maoist — 1969)

concepts.name: CPI and the Emergency (1975–77): A Controversial Alliance
key_dimensions: CPI supported Indira Gandhi's Emergency declaration — justified it as necessary against 'reactionary' and 'fascist' RSS-backed opposition
CPI(M) opposed the Emergency — key distinction from CPI's position
CPI's alliance with Congress during Emergency seen as opportunistic capitulation to authoritarianism
Long-term electoral consequence: CPI lost significant credibility and cadre base; CPI(M) benefited from being on the 'right side' of history

concepts.name: Naxalbari Uprising (1967) and Birth of CPI(ML)
key_dimensions: Peasant uprising in Naxalbari, West Bengal (1967) inspired by Mao's agrarian revolutionary model
Led by Charu Majumdar and Kanu Sanyal; rejected parliamentary path entirely — 'annihilation of class enemies' line
Formation of CPI(ML) in 1969 — further fragmentation of Indian Communist movement
UPSC trap: Naxalism emerged from within CPI(M), not directly from CPI; the split was CPI → CPI(M) → CPI(ML) in sequential stages

concepts.name: CPI's Trade Union Arm: AITUC and Labor Mobilization
key_dimensions: All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) — founded 1920, initially a broad platform, later dominated by CPI
UPSC trap: AITUC predates CPI's formal founding (1920 vs. 1925); it was not exclusively Communist at origin
Rivalry with INTUC (Congress-affiliated), HMS (Socialist), and CITU (CPI(M)-affiliated) — mapping trade union to political party affiliations
CPI's use of AITUC as organizational base for mobilizing industrial working class, especially in Bengal and Andhra

concepts.name: CPI's Ideological Evolution: From Revolution to 'National Democracy'
key_dimensions: CPI's 1951 Programme shift from armed insurrection (post-Telangana) to parliamentary path
Concept of 'National Democratic Revolution' — intermediate stage between bourgeois democracy and socialism, unique to CPI's Indian adaptation
CPI's acceptance of Nehru's 'socialist pattern of society' and support for public sector as progressive
Contrast with CPI(M)'s more independent 'People's Democratic Revolution' thesis — examinable ideological distinction

concepts.name: CPI and the National Question: Linguistic States and Nationality Theory
key_dimensions: CPI was among the earliest advocates for reorganization of states on linguistic basis — predating the States Reorganisation Act (1956)
Applied Stalinist nationality theory domestically: each linguistic group as a 'nationality' deserving self-determination
CPI's Andhra thesis (1948) specifically demanded a separate Andhra state — contributed to the broader linguistic reorganization demand
UPSC trap: CPI's support for linguistic states was ideologically driven (Stalinist theory), not merely cultural nationalism

concepts.name: S.A. Dange: Role, Controversies, and Legacy
key_dimensions: Dange as one of CPI's foremost leaders, AITUC president, and chief proponent of pro-Soviet parliamentary line
'Dange Letters' controversy (1964): alleged letters showing Dange offered to become a British informer — used to discredit him by CPI(M) faction
Dange faction retained the name 'CPI' after 1964 split while the other faction became CPI(M)
His position on Emergency (supporting it) further isolated him within the broader left — symbol of CPI's ideological compromises

concepts.name: EMS Namboodiripad: Theoretical Contributions and Political Legacy
key_dimensions: EMS as Kerala's first Chief Minister (1957–59) and again (1967–69) — two stints with different political contexts
Theoretical work: 'The National Question in Kerala' and analysis of caste-class intersections in Indian society
EMS's role in CPI(M) formation and his articulation of 'People's Democratic Revolution' as distinct from CPI's National Democracy thesis
Kerala model: CPI(M) under EMS associated with high human development indices — used in contemporary debates on alternative development

concepts.name: CPI in Post-1990 India: Decline, Coalition Politics, and Relevance
key_dimensions: Collapse of Soviet Union (1991) as ideological and material blow to pro-Soviet CPI
CPI's participation in United Front governments (1996–98) and UPA (2004–08) — 'outside support' model and eventual withdrawal over nuclear deal
UPSC trap: CPI and CPI(M) are distinct parties in coalition arithmetic — CPI generally smaller and more willing to align with Congress
Shrinking electoral base: from principal opposition (1952) to marginal force — reasons including fragmentation, identity politics rise, and ideological obsolescence debate
